chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Asbaat, from Muhammad ibn Uzafir, from his father who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) gave my father one thousand and seven hundred dinars, so he (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Trade with these'. Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'Know that there is no real interest for me in its profits, although the profits are desirable in it, but I loved that Allah, Majestic and Mighty, would see me exposing myself to its benefits'.

He (the narrator) said, 'So I made a gain of one hundred dinars for him in it. Then I met him, so I said to him, 'I have made a gain for you in it, of one hundred dinars'. So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was happy with that with an intense happiness, and he (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Corroborate it in the capital of my wealth'.

He (the narrator) said, 'So my father died and the wealth was with him. So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) sent a message to me, writing: 'May Allah grant us and you good health. There is for me with your father Muhammad, one thousand and eight hundred dinars, I had given him to trade with. So hand it over to Umar ibn Yazeed'.

He (the narrator) said, 'So I looked in the book of my father, so there was in it for Abu Musa, with me, a thousand and seven hundred dinars, and I had profited for him in it by one hundred dinars which Abdullah ibn Sinan and Umar ibn Yazeed both knew of it'.

key_terms.دِينَار: A gold coin used as currency in Islamic economic transactions
key_terms.مُتَعَرِّضاً: Exposing oneself or making oneself susceptible to

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the Imam's reaction to the trade profit in this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the concept of *istidraj* or divine facilitation in commerce, where Imam al-Sadiq (as) provided capital not for immediate gain, but to demonstrate the virtue of exposing oneself to Allah's bounty (*muta'arridan li-fawaidihi*). The narrative underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on meticulous record-keeping (*kitabat*) in financial dealings to ensure transparency and trust, as evidenced by the detailed accounting of profits and the subsequent transfer of assets to Umar ibn Yazid. It serves as a practical model for believers to view trade as a means of spiritual proximity and divine favor rather than mere material accumulation.
